units.title: The Nervous System
units.intro:
Neuron: dendrites collect, cell body integrates, axon carries the impulse, myelin speeds it in many fibres, synaptic knobs dump transmitter onto the next cell. Types: sensory (in), relay (middle), motor (out to muscle/gland).

**CNS** = brain + spinal cord. **PNS** = nerves to the rest. Reflex arc: receptor → sensory → relay (often in spinal cord) → motor → effector. Fast and does not wait for the brain to debate — you still become aware a moment later.

cards.title: 8.1.1 Structure and Characteristics of a Neurons
body: The nervous system is composed of billions of cells, the most basic structure being the nerve cell or neuron.
Neurons or nerve cells that underlie all the activities of the nervous system form a communication network that co-ordinates all the systems of the body.
A typical neuron has all the parts that any cell would have, and a few specialized structures that make it different.
The main portion of the nerve cell is called the **soma or cell body**.

cards.title: 8.1.2 Types of Neurons
body: Neurons that conduct messages from the sense organs to the brain or spinal cord are called sensory (afferent) neurons.
Different sensory neurons are sensitive to variety of stimuli.
The dendrites of a sensory neuron are usually part of a receptor.
Neurons that conduct messages from the brain or spinal cord to the muscles and glands are called motor (efferent) neurons.

cards.title: 8.1.3 Nerve Impulses
body: Nerves send impulses in response to stimuli.
Every neuron needs a certain minimum amount of stimulus in order to begin transmitting an impulse.
If the stimulus is greater than the threshold, the neuron will respond by sending an impulse.
If the stimulus continues, the neuron will continue to send impulses, one after the other.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which specific region of the human brain contains vital autonomic reflex centers that control breathing rate, heart rate, and blood vessel diameter?

steps.text: **Given:** Autonomic respiratory and cardiovascular control centers in the brain.

**Concepts:** The medulla oblongata, located at the lowest part of the brainstem, contains critical reflex centers (respiratory center and cardiac center) that manage essential life-support processes.
The cerebrum is for conscious thought and voluntary motor control.
The cerebellum coordinates movement and physical balance.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What chemical substance is released by stimulated parasympathetic postganglionic nerve fibers to reduce heart rate?

steps.text: **Concepts:** Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers release acetylcholine (ACh) onto target organs.
ACh binds to muscarinic receptors on cardiac muscle cells, reducing the heart rate.
Noradrenaline is released by postganglionic sympathetic fibers (elevates heart rate).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following behavioral patterns is characterized by a rapid, irreversible attachment formed to a moving object during a specific critical period early in life?
cards.why:
**Given:** Early life developmental behavioral adaptations.

**Concepts:** Imprinting is a highly restricted, rapid form of learning occurring during a sensitive period (critical window) shortly after birth/hatching that is generally irreversible.

**Steps:**
1. Habituation is learning to ignore irrelevant stimuli.
2. Imprinting is the rapid, irreversible attachment behavior.
3. Conditioning is associative over repeated trials.

**Final Result:** **Imprinting** is the correct behavioral term.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A cockroach running away from a sudden source of light is demonstrating which of the following inborn behaviors?
cards.why:
**Given:** Insect behavioral response to light.

**Concepts:** Taxis is a directed locomotory movement towards (positive) or away from (negative) a stimulus. Light stimulation is represented by 'photo'. Therefore, moving away from light is negative phototaxis.

**Steps:**
1. Running away indicates a 'negative' directional response.
2. The stimulus is light, which represents 'photo'.
3. Combining these yields negative phototaxis.

**Final Result:** **Negative Phototaxis** is the correct behavior.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The function of myelin sheath in the nervous system is primarily to

options.C: insulate nerve fibers and speed up electrical impulses.
options.E: repair damaged tissues in the brain.

cards.why: The **myelin sheath** is a fatty, insulating layer that surrounds the axons of many neurons. Its primary role is to electrically insulate the nerve fiber, which allows electrical impulses (action potentials) to travel much faster along the neuron.

lessons.title: Parts of the Human Nervous System

cards.title: Reflex recipe
body: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → CNS relay → motor neuron → effector → response. Skip “the brain thought about it” unless they ask about voluntary action.

cards.title: More detail — impulse and brain regions
body: Impulse is a travelling change of ions across the membrane, not a wire of flowing electrons. At the synapse the electrical story becomes chemical (transmitter) then electrical again — one-way traffic. Myelin + nodes = faster jump.

Cerebrum: thinking, sensing, voluntary move. Cerebellum: timing of movement / balance. Medulla: breathing and heart rate. Spinal cord: cable + reflex centre. Autonomic: automatic to guts and glands (sympathetic “go”, parasympathetic “rest”) — enough for this grade.
Learned behaviour needs experience; inborn does not. Reflex is inborn and stereotyped. Conditioning is learned association.

cards.title: 8.2.1 The Central Nervous System
body: Brain size is related to body size; larger brains are associated with larger bodies and not with greater intelligence.
The brain,part of the CNS, is housed within the cranium or skull cavity.
In vertebrate embryos, the brain begins developing very early.
The bony skull and three membranes, called the meninges, enclose the brain and protect it.

cards.title: 8.2.2 The Peripheral Nervous System
body: Even though the central nervous system (CNS) receives sensory information, evaluates the information and initiates action, without the peripheral nervous system (PNS), the CNS would remain isolated from both the body and the rest of the world.
The PNS collects information from numerous sources, both inside and outside the body, and relays it by way of afferent nerves to the CNS.
Without the PNS, the CNS would receive no sensory information and could produce no responses.
Even thoughts and emotions could not be expressed because of the CNS’s isolation from various parts of the body.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which specific region of the human brain contains vital autonomic reflex centers that control breathing rate, heart rate, and blood vessel diameter?
cards.why:
**Given:** Autonomic respiratory and cardiovascular control centers in the brain.

**Concepts:** The medulla oblongata, located at the lowest part of the brainstem, contains critical reflex centers (respiratory center and cardiac center) that manage essential life-support processes.

**Steps:**
1. The cerebrum is for conscious thought and voluntary motor control.
2. The cerebellum coordinates movement and physical balance.
3. The medulla oblongata houses the reflex pathways for cardiovascular and respiratory autonomic homeostatic regulation.

**Final Result:** **Medulla Oblongata** is the correct integration center.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What chemical substance is released by stimulated parasympathetic postganglionic nerve fibers to reduce heart rate?
cards.why:
**Given:** Autonomic neurotransmitter pathways.

**Concepts:** Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers release acetylcholine (ACh) onto target organs. ACh binds to muscarinic receptors on cardiac muscle cells, reducing the heart rate.

**Steps:**
1. Noradrenaline is released by postganglionic sympathetic fibers (elevates heart rate).
2. Acetylcholine is released by postganglionic parasympathetic fibers (lowers heart rate).

**Final Result:** **Acetylcholine** is the correct neurotransmitter.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When a **parasympathetic** and **sympathetic** nerve are stimulated the ______and _____chemical substance are released respectively
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify neurotransmitters.** The Autonomic Nervous System uses specific chemicals (neurotransmitters) to send signals.
**Step 2: Assign chemicals to systems.** 
- **Parasympathetic system** (Rest and Digest) primarily uses **acetylcholine**.
- **Sympathetic system** (Fight or Flight) primarily uses **noradrenaline** (norepinephrine).
**Step 3: Respectively.** The order must be Parasympathetic first, then Sympathetic. So, Acetylcholine and Noradrenaline.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: In humans, the center for regulating the amount of oxygen in the blood is situated at  A) cerebellum  B) medulla  C) cerebrum  D) hypothalamus  E) thalamus

steps.text:
**Step 1.** **Step 1: Identify brain regions and their functions.**
- **Cerebrum:** Thinking, memory, voluntary movement.
- **Cerebellum:** Balance and coordination.
- **Hypothalamus:** Hunger, thirst, temperature.
- **Medulla (oblongata):** Controls involuntary vital functions like heartbeat and **breathing** (by monitoring $$CO_2$$ and $$O_2$$ levels).

cards.title: Patterns of Behaviour
body: Inborn behaviour (instinct, reflex) vs learned (habit, conditioning, insight). The book wants examples, not slogans.

cards.title: 8.3.1 Inborn Behaviour
body: Inborn behaviour (innate behaviour) does not seem to be influenced by the wide range of environmental differences that exists among individuals.
Taxes (singular: taxis, meaning “movement”) Taxis is a locomotory response of motile cells, like a gamete or whole organism, in response to an external stimulus.
Taxis can be a positive or negative response.
For example the movement of a paramecium toward an acidic region is a positive taxis (positive chemotaxis) and the movement of a cockroach away from light is a negative taxis (negative phototaxis).

cards.title: 8.3.2 Learned Behaviour
body: **Learning** is an experience-based modification of behaviour.
Learning is characterized by flexibility: what is learned may vary from one individual to another, and the resulting behaviour may be modified if the environment changes.
Certainly, a learned behaviour pattern cannot be inherited, though the ability to learn is almost certainly inherited.
Individuals may improve learned behaviour over time.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the name of the outer protective membrane layer of flattened cells surrounding the axons of some peripheral neurons that facilitates axonal regeneration?
cards.why:
**Given:** Glial coverings of PNS neurons.

**Concepts:** The Schwann's sheath (neurilemma) is the outer nucleated layer of Schwann cells that surrounds the myelin sheath. It plays a critical role in regenerating damaged peripheral axons.

**Steps:**
1. Myelin sheath provides electrical insulation.
2. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in myelin.
3. Schwann's sheath is the outermost layer of Schwann cells that enables PNS axonal regeneration.

**Final Result:** **Schwann’s Sheath (Neurilemma)** is the correct anatomical structure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is primarily established and maintained by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Passive diffusion of sodium ions into the cell
options.B: Active transport of sodium and potassium ions by the sodium-potassium pump
options.C: Rapid opening of voltage-gated calcium channels
options.D: Enzymatic degradation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft

cards.why:
**Given:** Ionic transport mechanisms in excitable membranes.

**Concepts:** The resting membrane potential ($$-70.00\text{ mV}$$) is actively maintained by the sodium-potassium pump ($$\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$$ ATPase), which pumps $$3\text{ Na}^+$$ out of the cell for every $$2\text{ K}^+$$ pumped in, burning ATP.

**Steps:**
1. Passive diffusion would dissipate the potential gradient over time.
2. The resting potential requires active electrochemical gradient building.
3. The primary active transporter is the sodium-potassium pump.

**Final Result:** **Active transport of sodium and potassium ions by the sodium-potassium pump** is the correct mechanism.

steps.text: **Given:** Ionic transport mechanisms in excitable membranes.

**Concepts:** The resting membrane potential ($$-70.00\text{ mV}$$) is actively maintained by the sodium-potassium pump ($$\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$$ ATPase), which pumps $$3\text{ Na}^+$$ out of the cell for every $$2\text{ K}^+$$ pumped in, burning ATP.

**Steps:**
1. Passive diffusion would dissipate the potential gradient over time.
2. The resting potential requires active electrochemical gradient building.
3. The primary active transporter is the sodium-potassium pump.
**Final Result:** **Active transport of sodium and potassium ions by the sodium-potassium pump** is the correct mechanism.

cards.answer: Active transport of sodium and potassium ions by the sodium-potassium pump

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A newly hatched gosling follows the first moving object it sees. This behaviour is called ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Imprinting is rapid learning that happens during a short sensitive period early in life.

**Step 2:** The young animal forms an attachment, usually to its mother.

**Step 3:** Reflexes are automatic responses; habituation is learning to ignore a repeated stimulus.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: The long fibre of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body.
The lowest part of the brain stem; it controls automatic actions such as breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.
Associative learning is the ability of animals to associate one stimulus with another.
Behaviour refers to the responses that an organism gives in reaction to signals (stimuli) from its environment.
The main organ of the central nervous system, inside the skull, that controls body activities, thought and memory.
A nerve cell, specialised to carry electrical impulses.
The part of the brain at the back of the skull that coordinates movement and balance ("little brain").
A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought, e.g. pulling the hand from a hot object.
A short, branched extension of a neuron that receives impulses and carries them towards the cell body.
The spinal cord is a tube-like mass of nerve tissue, about 1.3 cm in diameter, although it is not uniform throughout its length.
Imprinting is a form of learning that is limited to a specific time period in animal’s life that is generally irreversible.
A synapse is the small space between two adjacent neurons.
Inborn behaviour is inherited and is an automatic behaviour pattern in animals, in which either the whole body or part of the animal moves either toward or away from a stimulus.
A movement of a whole organism or cell towards or away from a stimulus such as light or a chemical.
A part of the forebrain below the cerebrum that relays sensory messages to the cerebral cortex.
Chemotaxis is the tendency of cells (e.g. white blood cells) to migrate in the direction of a specific chemical stimulus given from the site of injury or infection.
Simple reflex behaviour is the simplest form of reflex, which does not depend on learning.
Learning is an experience-based modification of behaviour.

tips.text: The nervous system is composed of nerve cells or neurons.
Neurons are broadly categorized into three types, based on their functions in the body. These are sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons.
Sensory neurons transmit the messages they receive from receptors to the brain or spinal cord through a synapse.
Neurons use neurotransmitters to communicate with each other.
The majority of the human body’s functions are controlled by the nervous system.
The central nervous system comprises the brain and the spinal cord. These two organs receive impulses from sensory nerves, and interpret them.
The brain and the spinal cord transmit impulses that co-ordinate all the activities of the body via the motor nerves.
The brain is found within the cranium or skull cavity.
The brain consists of different parts, including the cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla, thalamus and hypothalamus.
The cerebrum, the largest portion of the brain, is divided into the left and right hemispheres.
